clue.text: Sharp pat 'and rub, perhaps ?

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words pat and rub may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A brisk pat and a rub, as a masseur might give.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the anagram of PAT RUB; 'and' only joins the two fodder words.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp turn or manner is a sudden, curt one.

clue.text: It entitled the old squire to rise

definitions.text: It entitled the old squire to rise

parts.words: It entitled the old squire to rise
parts.note: the touch of a sword on the shoulder made a kneeling squire a knight, giving him a title as he rose

explanation.surface: Something that once let a country gentleman stand up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entitled' means gave a title: the dubbing made the squire Sir.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial tap of the sword in knighting is the original sense of this word for an honour.

clue.text: Rob's not about in Herts

parts.note: Rob Roy was the Scottish outlaw, so Rob's other name gives Roy's

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word not is read backwards

explanation.surface: A thief's absence from Hertfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Royston is a market town in Hertfordshire (Herts), an English county north of London. 'about' turns NOT into TON.
explanation.definitionFit: The defining phrase points to a place within the county, and this market town lies on its northern edge.

clue.text: Hamlet's soul, so-called

parts.note: Hamlet, learning from the ghost that his uncle killed his father, cries 'O my ... soul!', the word for his soul's foreknowledge

explanation.surface: What the Danish prince called his own spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 Scene 5 Hamlet exclaims 'O my prophetic soul! My uncle!'
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's word for a soul that had foreseen the truth means foretelling the future.

clue.text: Figures for this month that's past, and two quarters

parts.note: the puzzle appeared in October, abbreviated Oct
something past happened ago
N for north is one quarter of the compass
S for south is a second compass quarter

explanation.surface: Accounts for the month just gone, with two quarterly sums added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' looks like sums in a ledger, but it is geometric figures; 'quarters' are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: An eight-sided shape is a plane figure in geometry.

clue.text: The city inn for the Merseyside skittle-player?

definitions.text: The city inn for the Merseyside skittle-player?

parts.words: The city inn for the Merseyside skittle-player?
parts.note: an old Fleet Street tavern in the City of London, and also the disc thrown at skittles, called a cheese, from the county that then reached the Mersey

explanation.surface: A London pub chosen by a bowler from the north-west.
explanation.walkthrough: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is a famous pub off Fleet Street; in skittles the disc thrown is a 'cheese', and Cheshire then bordered the Mersey.
explanation.definitionFit: A Fleet Street tavern bears the name of the crumbly county cheese, which doubles as the skittles missile.

clue.text: Tint forever novel

parts.note: a yellowish-brown tint, and the colour that follows Forever in the title of Kathleen Winsor's 1944 bestselling novel

explanation.surface: A colour that stays new for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forever Amber' was a racy historical novel of 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: The orange-yellow fossil-resin colour gives the title of the novel Forever Amber.

clue.text: Rough sleeper, apart from the rest

definitions.meaning: one who lies out of doors at night
something lying away from the main body or group

explanation.surface: A tramp who keeps away from everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lies outdoors sleeps rough, and a point that lies outside the main group is detached from it.

clue.text: Minor branches of the nobility

parts.note: small twigs, and also the young offspring of noble families, the phrase 'a sprig of the nobility'

explanation.surface: Junior lines of an aristocratic family tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor' suggests junior family lines; it is also small twigs, and 'minors' are the young.
explanation.definitionFit: Small shoots of a plant also stand for young scions of a noble house.

clue.text: Paper for drawing on — not in red !

definitions.text: Paper for drawing on — not in red

parts.words: Paper for drawing on — not in red
parts.note: a document a traveller draws money against at a bank, implying an account in the black rather than overdrawn

explanation.surface: Sketching paper, but don't use the red crayon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawing' looks like sketching; it is drawing money, and 'in red' means overdrawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank's written authority lets the holder withdraw funds up to a set sum.

clue.text: Heber's example of vile insularity

parts.note: Bishop Heber's hymn says of Ceylon's isle that every prospect pleases and only man is vile, so the vile islander is a native of that isle

explanation.surface: A hymn writer's instance of a nasty island character.
explanation.walkthrough: Reginald Heber's missionary hymn 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains' has the lines 'Blow soft o'er Ceylon's isle ... And only man is vile'.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Ceylon, the old name of Sri Lanka, is the islander the hymn calls vile.

clue.text: One of the 'canine tribe

parts.note: reads as a dog, but canines are also teeth, and every tooth bites

explanation.surface: A member of the dog family.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'canine tribe' suggests dogs; a canine is also a pointed tooth, a thing that bites.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that snaps, or a tooth that chews, is something that bites.

clue.text: Shut the door, d'you hear ? Use the thong

indicators.note: the question asks the solver to listen to how the order sounds when spoken

parts.note: to shut a door is to latch it

explanation.surface: A gruff order to close the door and then use a strap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latch it!' said quickly sounds like the old word for a shoe strap.
explanation.definitionFit: A latchet is an old word for the strap that fastens a shoe or sandal.

clue.text: Scots caller, fresh from the sea

definitions.text: Scots caller, fresh from the sea

parts.words: Scots caller, fresh from the sea
parts.note: in Scots 'caller' means fresh, and the Edinburgh fishwives' cry and song is 'Caller herrin'', fresh fish just landed

explanation.surface: A Scottish visitor arriving straight off a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caller' looks like a visitor or a telephone caller; in Scots it is an adjective meaning fresh, as in the song 'Caller Herrin''.
explanation.definitionFit: The silver fish sold fresh by Scottish fishwives is the one named in their street cry.

clue.text: Drake's enemy comes at Glamorgan's saint

parts.note: Sir Francis Drake fought the Spanish, and a Spanish gentleman is a Don

explanation.surface: Drake's Spanish foe turns up in South Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: St Donat's is a village and castle in the Vale of Glamorgan, named after the saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Donat gives his name to a Glamorgan parish and castle, so he is that county's patron there.

clue.text: Underdone turkey ? That's not common

parts.note: underdone meat is rare
a turkey is a bird

explanation.surface: A half-cooked turkey is an unusual thing at dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seldom met with is an unusual specimen, a phrase for anything uncommon.

clue.text: But the players sit here

parts.note: the paradox of a stand where the musicians sit down to play

explanation.surface: Yet the performers take seats in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'But' points at the contradiction: it is called a stand, yet the band sits there.
explanation.definitionFit: A park's raised, roofed platform is where a brass band performs.

clue.text: Church divisions risk money

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it
L and S stand for pounds and shillings, old British money

explanation.surface: Church factions gamble with their funds.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was pounds, shillings and pence, written L s d.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of a church near the altar, set apart for clergy and choir, is a division of the building.

clue.text: A remedy, of a kind

definitions.meaning: a medicine aimed at one particular disease
particular to one sort or type

explanation.surface: A cure that suits a particular sort of complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Old medicine called a targeted cure by this name; as an adjective it means belonging to one particular type.

clue.text: It's handy to have two common friends

parts.note: pal is an everyday word for a friend
mate is another everyday word for a friend

explanation.surface: Having a couple of ordinary friends comes in useful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handy' looks like useful; it means shaped like a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf with lobes spreading from one point like fingers is called hand-shaped.

clue.text: So the horse refuses ?

parts.note: a horse's call sounds like nay, the old word for no, as if the animal were refusing

explanation.surface: Is that how a horse says no?
explanation.walkthrough: The horse's cry sounds like 'nay', so its refusal is its whinny.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's whinny is its call, which sounds like an old word for no.

clue.text: Repeat tea rite with a difference

indicators.note: the letters of tea rite are presented again in a different order

explanation.surface: Perform the tea ceremony again, but differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a difference' signals the anagram of TEA RITE.
explanation.definitionFit: To do or say something over again is to say it once more.

clue.text: It just makes you sick!

parts.note: reads as an exclamation of disgust, but literally describes a substance that causes vomiting

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry at something infuriating.
explanation.walkthrough: The exasperated phrase is meant literally: the thing's whole purpose is to make you vomit.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug given to induce vomiting exists for that one purpose.

clue.text: Damage round lake retreat on the Indian coast

indicators.note: the word for damage goes round the reversed lake name

parts.note: to damage is to mar

indicators.note: to retreat is to go back, so the lake's name is read backwards

parts.note: Bala is the largest natural lake in Wales

explanation.surface: Harm done around a lakeside hideaway on India's shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' looks like a holiday hideaway but turns BALA into ALAB, which 'round' puts inside MAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The south-western shore of India is known as the Malabar Coast.

clue.text: Sanders's skeleton staff, on the river

definitions.text: Sanders's skeleton staff, on the river

parts.words: Sanders's skeleton staff, on the river
parts.note: Lieutenant ... is Sanders's assistant in Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories, and a skeleton is made of what his nickname says

explanation.surface: A colonial officer's minimal team on a river posting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skeleton staff' means a tiny team; here the skeleton is literal, and Bones is the comic aide in Wallace's 'Sanders of the River'.
explanation.definitionFit: A skeleton consists of the hard framework pieces, which give the nickname of Sanders's aide.

clue.text: At his work, night and day, this artist

definitions.text: At his work, night and day, this artist

parts.words: At his work, night and day, this artist
parts.note: reads as a tireless worker, but Night and Day are two of the sculptor's carvings on London Transport's Broadway headquarters

explanation.surface: A painter who labours round the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Epstein carved the figures 'Night' and 'Day' for 55 Broadway in London in 1929.
explanation.definitionFit: The sculptor Jacob of that surname made carved figures titled Night and Day.

clue.text: Mark II, obsolete

parts.note: Mark is the first name of the American author, and II is two, for which the archaic word is his pen-name surname

explanation.surface: A second model, now out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark II' looks like a superseded model; it is Mark plus the archaic word for two, giving Mark Twain.
explanation.definitionFit: The old poetic word for two is also the surname Samuel Clemens took as an author.

clue.text: Run down, Diana has to box her years (sic)

parts.note: Di is short for Diana
to spar is to box
a person's years are her age

explanation.surface: A tired woman takes up boxing at her age, the setter noting the odd grammar.
explanation.walkthrough: '(sic)' admits the clumsy surface; it gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To run something down is to belittle it.

clue.text: Torches have points in heraldic devices

indicators.note: the compass points go inside the heraldic devices

parts.note: crests are heraldic devices
S and E are compass points, south and east

explanation.surface: Flaming brands bearing spikes on coats of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: A cresset is an iron basket of burning fuel used as a torch or beacon.

clue.text: Venomous snakes on the increase

parts.note: the poisonous snakes are also those who add, people forever increasing a total

explanation.surface: Poisonous serpents multiplying.
explanation.walkthrough: The snakes, read another way, are people or machines that add, always making things bigger.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's only venomous snake shares its name with anyone who sums figures.
